title: How Does a Split System Air Conditioner Work?
h1: How Does a Split System Air Conditioner Work?
description: A split system puts the noisy compressor outside and the coil and blower inside. Here's how the two halves work together to cool your whole home.
quick_answer: A split system air conditioner has two halves. The outdoor unit holds the compressor and condenser coil. The indoor unit holds the evaporator coil and a blower. Refrigerant lines connect them, carrying heat from inside your house to the outdoor unit, where it's released. The indoor blower sends the cooled air through ducts or out of a wall unit.
body:
What are the two parts of a split system?

The name comes from splitting the equipment into an outdoor section and an indoor section. That setup keeps the loudest part, the compressor, outside your living space.

  • Outdoor unit (condenser): the compressor, a large coil and a fan. It sits on a pad beside the house or sometimes on a roof.
  • Indoor unit: an evaporator coil plus a blower. In ducted homes this is usually a furnace or air handler in the attic, garage or a hall closet. In ductless homes it's a head mounted on the wall.
  • Line set: two copper refrigerant lines, plus control wiring, running between the two.
  • Thermostat: tells both halves when to start and stop.

How does a split AC actually cool the air?

An air conditioner doesn't make cold. It moves heat out of the house. The refrigerant does that by absorbing heat when it evaporates and giving it off when it condenses.

  1. The blower pulls warm room air through the return grille and across the indoor coil.
  2. Cold refrigerant inside that coil absorbs heat from the air. The air leaves cooler and travels through the ducts to each room.
  3. The refrigerant, now carrying that heat, flows through the larger copper line to the outdoor unit.
  4. The compressor raises its pressure and temperature so it's hotter than the outside air.
  5. The outdoor fan blows air across the condenser coil, and the heat leaves the refrigerant.
  6. The refrigerant passes through an expansion device, gets cold again, and returns indoors to repeat the loop.

Along the way, moisture in your indoor air condenses on the cold coil and drains away through a condensate line. That's why a working AC also dries the air a bit.

Ducted split vs. ductless mini-split: what's the difference?

Both are split systems. The difference is how the cool air gets to you.

A ducted split uses one indoor air handler or furnace and a network of ducts. It's the most common central air setup in San Diego and Orange County tract homes, with the ducts running through the attic.

A ductless mini-split skips the ducts. A small refrigerant line runs from the outdoor unit to one or more wall or ceiling units, each with its own blower and its own temperature setting. Mini-splits work well for room additions, converted garages, older homes with no ductwork, and rooms that never seem to cool down.

Can a split system also heat?

Yes, in two ways. A standard split AC is often paired with a gas furnace that shares the same blower and ducts. The AC coil sits on top of the furnace, and the system uses the furnace for heat and the AC for cooling.

Or the outdoor unit can be a heat pump, which runs the refrigerant cycle in reverse to bring heat indoors in winter. Most ductless mini-splits sold today are heat pumps, so a single system covers both seasons.

What keeps a split system working well?

Most problems we find come from airflow, coil condition or refrigerant. A few habits help:

  • Change or clean the filter on schedule, and more often during Santa Ana winds or wildfire smoke.
  • Keep two feet of clear space around the outdoor unit. Trim shrubs and move stored items.
  • Near the coast, gently hose off the outdoor coil now and then to rinse salt and dust. Turn the power off first.
  • Watch the condensate drain. Water around the indoor unit or a stuck float switch usually means a clog.
  • Book a yearly tune-up before the hot inland months so a technician can check refrigerant pressures, electrical parts and coil cleanliness.

Refrigerant handling requires certification and special equipment, so leave anything involving the line set, compressor or electrical panel to a technician.

Is a split system the right choice for my home?

For most single-family homes with existing ductwork, a ducted split system is the straightforward pick. If your ducts are in rough shape, or you only need to cool part of the house, a mini-split may make more sense. faqs: Why is it called a split system?

Because the equipment is split between an outdoor unit, which holds the compressor and condenser coil, and an indoor unit, which holds the evaporator coil and blower. A packaged unit, by contrast, puts everything in one cabinet.
Is a split system quieter than a window unit?
Usually, yes. The compressor, which makes most of the noise, sits outside. Indoors you mostly hear the blower and air moving through the vents.
How often should a split system be serviced?
Once a year is a good baseline, ideally in spring before the hot months. If it's a heat pump that runs year-round, some homeowners prefer a check in both spring and fall.
Can I add a mini-split to a house that already has central air?
Yes. People often add a mini-split for a hot upstairs room, an addition or a converted garage. It runs on its own and doesn't change how your central system works.
